title: An escape line rebuilt after every arrest, from a Brussels apartment to a British car in Spain
summary: A downed airman was worth more flying again than hidden in an attic, so a chain of households, forgers and Basque guides moved him from a Belgian farmhouse to a British diplomatic car in Spain, each link knowing only the one before and after. Andrée de Jongh's route and Michael Creswell's money turned scattered civilian rescue into a single accountable system; German and collaborationist counter-agents broke it at least four times, and each time survivors rebuilt it, until in 1944 railway bombing and the invasion turned the last of it into forest camps waiting for the Allied line to arrive.

nodes.name: Brussels
nodes.note: The principal northern command, finance, documentation, shelter and sorting center. Airmen collected across the provinces were concealed, photographed, clothed and grouped here before the southbound journey; the Gestapo/Sipo-SD post on Avenue Louise and Saint-Gilles Prison sat in the same city.

nodes.name: Valenciennes
nodes.note: An early relay on the Belgian–French frontier belt, held by Charles Morelle and associated households, feeding parties onto the Paris trains after the crossing near Hertain, Tournai or Rumes.

nodes.name: Paris
nodes.note: The indispensable interchange: document production, replenishment, and the handoff between the Belgian and southern sectors, repeatedly destroyed by arrest and rebuilt. Frédéric de Jongh, the Aylés and Jacques Le Grelle each in turn ran it from here.

nodes.name: Bordeaux
nodes.note: A rail relay and occasional staging point between Paris and the Basque coast, used when the direct route was unsafe.

nodes.name: Bayonne
nodes.note: The southern urban interchange, run by the Dassié and Lapeyre families, providing reception, lodging and links onward to Anglet. Arrests in March 1943 severely damaged this node.

nodes.name: Anglet
nodes.note: The southern command and financial center, run from the household of Elvire and Fernand De Greef. Not a mere safe house: money, schedules, personnel and the relationship with Creswell were managed here, and the passage notebooks were kept in Elvire De Greef's custody.

nodes.name: Saint-Jean-de-Luz–Ciboure
nodes.note: Coastal relay before the classical Urrugne–Bidasoa passage, held by Kattalin Aguirre, where parties rested and changed clothing before the mountain stage.

nodes.name: Urrugne, Bidegain Berri
nodes.note: The final French safe-house belt on the classical route, run by Frantxia Usandizaga. Andrée de Jongh, three RAF airmen, Usandizaga and Juan Manuel Larburu were arrested here on 15 January 1943, ending the farm's use; the arresting agency and the informer are disputed.

nodes.name: Bidasoa crossing
nodes.note: The lethal final stage: a night river-and-mountain crossing near Endarlatsa or Behobia. Antoine d'Ursel drowned attempting it on 24 December 1943, proof that the landscape itself was a hazard independent of German patrols.

nodes.name: Oiartzun
nodes.note: First Spanish reception point after the crossing, where Basque helpers hid parties and notified the British contact, at continuous risk of Guardia Civil arrest.

nodes.name: San Sebastián
nodes.note: A transfer point on the road from the frontier to Bilbao, where British-linked intermediaries could take custody of authenticated evaders.

nodes.name: Bilbao
nodes.note: The original British-contact and accounting node: de Jongh met Michael Creswell here in August or September 1941 and secured the agreement that turned local rescue into a financed system.

nodes.name: Madrid
nodes.note: Diplomatic control point where the British embassy debriefed and moved authenticated aircrew under protection toward Gibraltar.

nodes.name: Gibraltar
nodes.note: The last node under British control before repatriation to Britain; once here, an evader ceased to be the network's operational responsibility.

nodes.name: Miranda de Ebro
nodes.note: The Spanish internment camp that swallowed the first, unsupported southbound attempt in summer 1941. Its use demonstrated that a frontier crossing alone was not a rescue, and forced the founders to seek diplomatic reception.

nodes.name: Fréteval Forest
nodes.note: The code-named Sherwood camps, organized by Jean de Blommaert from May 1944 when rail travel south became too costly and slow. Roughly 152–156 airmen were sheltered here until Allied forces, with Airey Neave, reached the camp on 13–14 August 1944.

nodes.name: Beffe
nodes.note: One of six small Belgian Ardennes camps (with Villance, Acremont, Porcheresse, Bellevaux and Bohan) built by Albert Ancia and Gaston Matthys to hide airmen until liberation. German searches forced an evacuation from Beffe toward Villance; four airmen were captured, showing Marathon was not uniformly secure.

nodes.name: The Comet Line
nodes.note: The corporate whole: a compartmented, volunteer relay that MI9 financed and authenticated but did not command outright. Its southern ledger securely identifies 288 Allied military evaders passed into Spain; broader memorial totals run to several hundred more, depending on category.

nodes.name: MI9 / IS9
nodes.note: The British organization behind escape-and-evasion policy, money, authentication and, from 1944, the shift to Marathon's forest concealment. Reorganized during the war under overlapping designations.

nodes.name: The passage notebooks
nodes.note: Three small notebooks begun after the Creswell agreement, recording successful Pyrenean passages as evidence for British reimbursement. They are the firmest quantitative record the network produced, and the reason the 288-person figure can be trusted where broader totals cannot.

nodes.name: Andrée de Jongh
nodes.note: Founder, route designer and negotiator with the British, known as Dédée and to MI9 as Postman. Arrested at Urrugne on 15 January 1943 and deported under Nacht und Nebel procedure; she survived. Personally escorted roughly 78 of the network's first 118 evaders.

nodes.name: Arnold Deppé
nodes.note: Cofounder and southwest-France specialist, whose prewar residence supplied the geography the line depended on. His arrest in late 1941 removed a founder and forced more caution.

nodes.name: Jacques Donny
nodes.note: Early treasurer and financier, drawing on private Belgian donors before British funding began. Arrested 1 December 1942, condemned to death in October 1943, executed at Stuttgart on 24 February 1944.

nodes.name: Frédéric de Jongh
nodes.note: Andrée's father, coordinator of the Paris sector and, after her arrest, overall head while southern crossings passed to Nothomb. Arrested with the Aylés in June 1943 and shot at Mont-Valérien on 28 March 1944.

nodes.name: Jean Greindl
nodes.note: Known as Nemo, rebuilt and directed the Brussels sector after the first arrest wave. Arrested on 6 February 1943 and died in Saint-Gilles Prison during an Allied bombing raid on 7 September 1943.

nodes.name: Jean-François Nothomb
nodes.note: Known as Franco, principal international guide and, after the 1943 leadership losses, overall controller of the southern route. Crossed to warn Creswell on 24 January 1943 and reopened the line by spring. Arrested in Paris in January 1944 and survived deportation.

nodes.name: Antoine d'Ursel
nodes.note: Known as Jacques Cartier, led the Belgian sector during 1943. Drowned attempting the Bidasoa crossing on 24 December 1943.

nodes.name: Elvire De Greef
nodes.note: Known as Tante Go, ran the Anglet hub through multiple northern collapses: money, schedules, southern personnel and the relationship with Creswell. Accompanied the last four evacuated airmen from liberated Biarritz to Britain on 28 September 1944.

nodes.name: Florentino Goikoetxea
nodes.note: Basque mountain guide whose route knowledge made him the network's most celebrated frontier specialist. Judged the Bidasoa unsafe to cross on the night of the January 1943 arrest and slept elsewhere, escaping capture. Wounded and captured in 1944 and later rescued.

nodes.name: Michael Creswell
nodes.note: Known as Timothy or Monday, the diplomatic and MI9 hinge who verified de Jongh's proposal, funded the line and passed instructions north. The agreement he reached with her in Bilbao is what converted local rescue into a system.

nodes.name: Micheline Dumon
nodes.note: Known as Michou, a courier and organizer who repeatedly restored broken northern and southern links and identified Jacques Desoubrie as a threat, escaping to Britain before capture.

nodes.name: Jacques Le Grelle
nodes.note: Known as Jérôme, sent from Britain in mid-1943 to reinforce the Paris sector. Arrested on 17 January 1944 during the collapse caused by Desoubrie's penetration; survived imprisonment.

nodes.name: Jean de Blommaert
nodes.note: Belgian officer parachuted back into France in April 1944 who organized the Fréteval concealment camps, converting a damaged transport network into distributed shelter for the final months.

nodes.name: Prosper Dezitter
nodes.note: Belgian collaborator and professional infiltrator, using false Allied identities and invented London contacts against Comète and other networks. Attributions of the arrests his group caused range from at least 700 (Belgium WWII) to disputed claims of 1,000 or 1,500. Convicted and executed in Belgium in 1948.

nodes.name: Jacques Desoubrie
nodes.note: German agent, operating as Jean Masson and other aliases, who penetrated transport and liaison connections and helped cause the January 1944 Paris and Brussels arrests. Claims of exactly 150 airmen, 250 helpers or over 1,000 persons betrayed are disputed aggregate figures. Captured, tried and executed in France in 1949.
